title: Toast and Crackers for a Hangover: Do Bland Carbs Help?
excerpt: Is toast good for a hangover? Why dry toast and saltine crackers settle a queasy stomach, how to eat them when you feel sick, the best toppings, and what they can't fix.
metaDescription: Is toast good for a hangover? Why toast and saltines settle a queasy stomach, how to eat them when nauseous, the best toppings, and what they can't fix.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** toast and crackers won't cure a hangover, but they are one of the most sensible first foods when your stomach is queasy the morning after drinking. Plain, dry carbohydrates are easy to keep down, they put something in an irritated stomach without adding fat or acid, and they give your body some easy fuel after a night when alcohol may have nudged your blood sugar down. That's a real but modest benefit. They don't speed up how fast your body clears alcohol, and they don't fix dehydration, poor sleep, or the inflammation behind a hangover.

**The quick plan:** If you feel sick, start with small sips of water or an electrolyte drink. Once that stays down for 15 to 30 minutes, nibble a few saltine crackers or half a slice of plain toast. Go slowly. When your stomach settles, move up to toast with a topping that adds protein or potassium, like peanut butter, a banana, or eggs. Save the greasy fry-up for later, if at all.

> **When to see a doctor.** Toast and crackers are for an ordinary rough morning, not for anything more serious. **Get medical help if** you can't keep any fluids down for more than about 12 hours, you're vomiting blood or something that looks like coffee grounds, you have severe or worsening belly pain, you're very dizzy or faint when you stand up, you've barely urinated all day, or you still feel very unwell after 24 hours. **Call 911 right away if** someone who has been drinking is confused, hard to wake, having a seizure, breathing slowly or irregularly, has blue-tinged lips or skin, or is vomiting while barely conscious. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, and food will not help. If you have diabetes, alcohol plus skipped meals can drop your blood sugar dangerously low, so check your glucose and follow your care plan. And if you get shaking, sweating, racing heart, or strong anxiety when you stop after drinking heavily every day for a while, that may be alcohol withdrawal rather than a hangover. Talk to a doctor about it, because withdrawal can be serious and is treatable.

## Is Toast Good for a Hangover?

Yes, as a starting point. Toast is popular for hangovers for the same reason it shows up on every "upset stomach" list: it is bland, low in fat, low in fiber (if you use white bread), and easy to digest. When your stomach is irritated, that's exactly what you want.

Here's what toast actually does for you on a hangover morning:

- **It's gentle on an irritated stomach.** Alcohol irritates the lining of the stomach and can increase acid production. Rich, fatty, spicy, or acidic foods can make that feel worse. Dry toast gives your stomach something to work on without much to react to.
- **It gives you easy carbohydrates.** Alcohol interferes with the liver's ability to make new glucose, which is why heavy drinking, especially on an empty stomach, can lower blood sugar. Simple carbs from toast are a quick way to top that up.
- **Toasting helps a little.** Toasting dries the bread out, so it's less doughy and sits a bit lighter. Many people find warm, dry toast easier to face than soft bread when they're nauseous. That's comfort, not chemistry, but it counts.
- **It's a platform for better food.** Plain toast is low in protein and most vitamins and minerals. Its real strength is that you can build on it once your stomach allows: eggs, peanut butter, banana, avocado.

What toast doesn't do: it doesn't "soak up" alcohol that is already in your bloodstream, it doesn't speed up your liver, and it doesn't rehydrate you. By the morning, most or all of the alcohol has usually already been absorbed and processed. You're dealing with the after-effects, and toast helps with only one slice of those (pun intended).

## Are Crackers Good for a Hangover?

Saltine crackers might be the single most reliable food for hangover nausea. They're dry, plain, small, and easy to eat in tiny amounts. You can eat one cracker, wait, and eat another. That kind of slow, controlled eating is exactly what a queasy stomach needs.

Why crackers work well:

- **Small portions are built in.** A single cracker is a few bites. It's easy to stop the moment your stomach complains, which is harder with a full slice of toast.
- **They're dry and starchy.** Starchy, dry food is a long-standing piece of advice for nausea of many kinds. Obstetric guidance for morning sickness, for example, has long suggested keeping dry crackers or toast nearby and eating a few before getting out of bed. The same idea applies when your stomach is unsettled after drinking.
- **They have a little salt.** Saltines contain a small amount of sodium. That won't replace much of what you lost, and a few crackers are no substitute for proper fluids, but salty food can make you want to drink, which is helpful.
- **They keep well.** You can stash a sleeve on your nightstand or in a bag. Eating a few before bed after a night out, along with a glass of water, is an easy habit.

Crackers have the same limits as toast. They're mostly refined starch with very little protein, fiber, potassium, or vitamins. They're a bridge food: something to get you from "can't face eating" to "ready for a real meal."

## Saltines vs Toast: Which Is Better When You're Hungover?

Both do the same basic job. The best choice depends on how you feel.

| | Saltine crackers | Plain toast |
|---|---|---|
| Best for | Active nausea, first food after vomiting | Mild queasiness, ready for a bit more |
| Portion control | Very easy (one at a time) | Harder (a slice is a bigger commitment) |
| Salt | A small amount | Little, unless salted butter or toppings |
| Toppings | Not really | Yes, easy to build into a meal |
| Convenience | Keeps for weeks, no prep | Needs bread and a toaster |
| Gluten-free option | Rice crackers, gluten-free crackers | Gluten-free bread |

A good sequence for a rough morning is **crackers first, toast second, real food third.** If even crackers feel like too much, stick with small sips of fluid for a while longer and try again in 30 minutes.

## Why Bland Carbs Help: The Science in Plain Words

There are three main reasons plain carbs make sense the morning after. One is well supported, one is partly supported, and one is mostly about comfort.

### 1. Your stomach is irritated

Alcohol is a direct irritant to the stomach lining. Heavy drinking can cause short-term inflammation of the stomach (acute gastritis), which shows up as nausea, a burning or gnawing ache, bloating, and sometimes vomiting. Alcohol can also slow down how quickly your stomach empties, which adds to that heavy, sloshing feeling.

When the stomach is in that state, foods that are fatty, spicy, acidic, or very rich tend to make symptoms worse. Fat in particular slows stomach emptying even further. Plain toast and crackers are about as low-effort as food gets. If burning pain is your main symptom, our guide to [stomach pain after drinking](/never-hungover/stomach-pain-after-drinking) goes deeper into what's going on and when it needs attention.

### 2. Alcohol can lower your blood sugar

This part is well established in physiology. Your liver normally keeps your blood sugar steady overnight, partly by making new glucose. Breaking down alcohol ties up the same chemical machinery the liver uses for that job, so while you're processing alcohol, it makes less new glucose. If you drank a lot, ate little, and then slept for hours, your blood sugar can dip.

Low blood sugar can cause shakiness, weakness, sweating, irritability, trouble focusing, and headache, which overlap a lot with hangover symptoms. Eating some easy carbohydrates is a quick and harmless way to address that.

The honest caveat: research on whether low blood sugar actually drives hangover severity is mixed. Studies that measured glucose in hungover people have not consistently found that it explains how bad they feel. So treat the blood-sugar benefit as a sensible bonus rather than the main event. The exception is people with diabetes, especially those on insulin or certain tablets, for whom alcohol-related low blood sugar is a genuine safety issue. Our [guide to alcohol and blood sugar](/never-hungover/alcohol-diabetes-blood-sugar-management-guide-2025) covers that in detail.

### 3. Eating something often helps nausea

Many people find that an empty stomach makes nausea worse, and that a small amount of bland food takes the edge off. This is common advice for nausea from many causes, and it lines up with a lot of personal experience, though it's not something that has been tested much in hangover studies specifically. If nausea is your main problem, our [complete guide to hangover nausea](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025) covers other options, including ginger, which has better research behind it for nausea in general. See our separate look at [ginger for hangovers](/never-hungover/ginger-for-hangover) for the details.

## Toast and the BRAT Diet

You may have heard of the BRAT diet: **B**ananas, **R**ice, **A**pplesauce, and **T**oast. It was long recommended for upset stomachs and diarrhea because all four foods are bland and easy to digest.

For a hangover, the BRAT foods are a reasonable starting point for a day or so. Each one brings something slightly different:

- **Bananas** add potassium and are soft and easy to eat. (Our [bananas for hangover](/never-hungover/bananas-for-hangover) guide covers what they can and can't do.)
- **Rice** is filling and very gentle.
- **Applesauce** is easy to swallow and has some natural sugar.
- **Toast** is the dry, starchy base.

The caveat is that BRAT foods are low in protein, fat, and many nutrients. Pediatric guidance has moved away from a strict BRAT diet for children with stomach bugs for that reason, favoring a return to a normal diet as soon as it's tolerated. The same logic applies to adults with a hangover: use bland foods to get started, then move back to normal meals once your stomach can handle them. You don't need to stay on toast all day.

## How to Eat Toast and Crackers When You're Hungover

How you eat matters as much as what you eat when you feel sick.

1. **Fluids first.** Start with small sips of water, an electrolyte drink, or a flat, non-caffeinated drink. If you've been vomiting, try a sip or two every few minutes rather than a big glass.
2. **Wait until fluids stay down.** Give it 15 to 30 minutes. If the water stays put, you're ready for food.
3. **Start very small.** One or two crackers, or a quarter to half a slice of dry toast. Chew slowly.
4. **Pause between bites.** Wait 10 to 15 minutes. If you still feel okay, have a bit more.
5. **Sit upright.** Lying flat right after eating can make nausea and reflux worse. Sit up or prop yourself on pillows for a while.
6. **Keep drinking.** Keep sipping fluids between bites. Toast and crackers are dry, and you need the water anyway.
7. **Step up when you can.** Once plain toast is sitting well, add a topping with protein or nutrients, and then move on to a normal meal.

If you can't keep anything down after several hours of trying, stop experimenting with food and see the "when to see a doctor" box at the top of this page.

## The Best Toast Toppings for a Hangover

Plain toast is the starting line, not the finish. Once your stomach has settled, toppings can turn toast into a more useful hangover breakfast.

### Good choices once you feel steadier

- **Eggs.** Scrambled, poached, or boiled eggs on toast add protein and are still fairly gentle. Eggs also contain cysteine, an amino acid often mentioned in hangover discussions, though the evidence that eating eggs reduces hangover symptoms is thin. Our [eggs for hangover](/never-hungover/eggs-for-hangover) page looks at that claim honestly.
- **Peanut or almond butter.** Adds protein and some fat, which helps you stay full. Use a thin layer at first, since fat is harder on a queasy stomach.
- **Sliced banana.** Adds potassium and natural sugar. Peanut butter and banana on toast is a classic for good reason.
- **Avocado.** Provides potassium and healthy fats. Again, go easy if you're still nauseous.
- **A little honey.** Adds quick sugar and tends to taste good when nothing else does. You'll sometimes read that the fructose in honey speeds up alcohol clearance. There is some old, small research on fructose and alcohol metabolism, but there is no good evidence that honey on toast meaningfully shortens a hangover.
- **Plain yogurt or cottage cheese on the side.** Easy protein that many people find soothing.

### Toppings to skip or delay

- **Lots of butter.** A thin scrape is fine. A thick layer adds a lot of fat to an irritated stomach.
- **Spicy spreads and hot sauce.** Can aggravate stomach irritation and heartburn.
- **Very acidic toppings.** Lots of tomato or citrus can bother an upset stomach or reflux.
- **A full greasy fry-up.** Bacon, sausage, and fried bread are a popular hangover tradition, but heavy fat slows stomach emptying and can make nausea worse. If you love a greasy breakfast, wait until your stomach has properly settled. The popular idea that grease "soaks up" alcohol doesn't hold up either, since by morning the alcohol is already absorbed.

## White, Whole Grain, or Sourdough?

When you're nauseous, **white bread is usually the easiest.** It's lower in fiber, which means it moves through the stomach more quickly and gives your stomach less to do.

Once you're feeling better, **whole grain bread is the more nourishing choice.** It has more fiber, B vitamins, and minerals, and its slower-release carbohydrates help keep your energy steadier through the day. Heavy drinking can deplete some B vitamins over time, so whole grains are a good habit in general.

**Sourdough** sits somewhere in between. Some people find it easier to digest, and it has a pleasant tang that can be welcome when your mouth tastes off. It's a fine choice if you like it.

If you're sensitive to gluten or have celiac disease, gluten-free bread, rice cakes, or rice crackers do the same job.

## What About Toast Before Drinking?

Eating before drinking is one of the best-supported ways to soften the next day. Food in your stomach slows down how quickly alcohol passes into your small intestine, where most of it is absorbed. That means a lower, slower peak in blood alcohol and less of a hit to your stomach lining.

But a slice of toast alone isn't much of a buffer. Bread doesn't "soak up" alcohol like a sponge. What helps is having a real meal in your stomach, ideally one with protein, some fat, fiber, and carbohydrates, because that combination keeps food in your stomach longer. Toast as part of a bigger meal is fine. Toast as your only food before a big night isn't going to do much.

For what to eat beforehand, see our evidence-based guide on [what to eat before drinking](/never-hungover/what-to-eat-before-drinking-alcohol-evidence-based-guide), and for why skipping food makes things worse, see [drinking on an empty stomach](/never-hungover/drinking-on-an-empty-stomach).

## Toast and Crackers Before Bed After a Night Out

Eating a few crackers or a slice of toast before bed, along with a big glass of water, is a reasonable habit after a night of drinking. It won't undo the evening, but it gives your stomach something besides alcohol, gives your body some carbs to work with overnight, and the salt in crackers may encourage you to drink a bit more water.

What it won't do is sober you up. Your liver clears alcohol at a fairly fixed rate, roughly one standard drink per hour for many people, and food eaten at the end of the night doesn't change that much. Never use a late-night snack as a reason to think you're okay to drive.

## What Toast and Crackers Can't Fix

It's worth being clear about the limits, so you know what else to do.

- **Dehydration.** Alcohol suppresses a hormone that helps your kidneys hold onto water, so you urinate more. Toast does nothing for this. Water, electrolyte drinks, or broth are what help. Our [comparison of electrolyte drinks for hangovers](/never-hungover/electrolyte-drinks-for-hangover-compared) can help you pick one.
- **Poor sleep.** Alcohol can make you fall asleep faster but disrupts sleep later in the night. Rest, if you can get it, matters more than breakfast.
- **Headache and body aches.** These are tied to inflammation, dehydration, and poor sleep, not just an empty stomach.
- **The overall hangover.** Researchers increasingly think hangovers involve the body's inflammatory response and the effects of acetaldehyde, a toxic by-product made when alcohol is broken down. No food has been shown to reliably fix those.

For a fuller look at what does and doesn't help, our [science-based guide to curing a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-cure-a-hangover-complete-science-guide) and our list of the [best foods for a hangover](/never-hungover/best-foods-for-hangover) are good next reads.

## A Simple Hangover Food Plan

Putting it all together, here's a realistic way to eat your way through a rough morning.

**Hour 0 to 1 (feeling rough):** Small sips of water or an electrolyte drink. Once those stay down, a few saltines or half a slice of dry toast.

**Hour 1 to 3 (settling down):** A full slice of toast, maybe with a thin layer of peanut butter or a few slices of banana. Keep sipping fluids. Ginger tea can help if nausea lingers.

**Hour 3 onward (hungry again):** A proper meal with protein and vegetables, such as eggs on whole grain toast, a rice bowl, or soup with bread. Keep drinking water through the afternoon.

**Later that day:** Back to normal meals. If you still can't keep food down by evening, or you feel worse rather than better, that's a reason to contact a doctor.

## Where Supplements Like DHM Fit

Toast and crackers help with the stomach side of a hangover. They do nothing for the alcohol metabolism side. That's where some people look at supplements, and it's worth being honest about where the science stands.

**DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a compound from the Japanese raisin tree (*Hovenia dulcis*) that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the research is in animals and lab studies, with only limited human data. It's promising but not settled, and there is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers in everyone or replaces drinking less, eating, and hydrating. If you want to try it alongside sensible habits, it's typically taken before or while drinking rather than the next morning. Popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands.

Whatever you do, the boring basics still matter most: pace your drinks, eat a real meal beforehand, alternate with water, and keep plain toast and crackers on hand for the morning after.

## The Bottom Line

Toast and crackers are a smart first food for a hangover, not a cure. They're bland, easy to keep down, gentle on an irritated stomach, and provide quick carbohydrates after alcohol may have lowered your blood sugar. Start with crackers if you're nauseous, move to toast, then build up to toast with protein or potassium-rich toppings, and get back to normal meals as soon as you can. Pair them with plenty of fluids, because dehydration is something no slice of bread can fix. And if you can't keep fluids down, have severe pain, or see signs of alcohol poisoning, skip the kitchen and get medical help.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is toast good for a hangover?**

Yes, as a first food. Plain toast is bland, low in fat, and easy to digest, so it's gentle on a stomach irritated by alcohol, and it provides quick carbohydrates after alcohol may have lowered your blood sugar. It won't cure a hangover or rehydrate you, so pair it with plenty of fluids and move on to more nourishing food once your stomach settles.

**Are saltine crackers good for a hangover?**

Saltines are one of the easiest foods to keep down when you're nauseous. They're dry, plain, and come in small portions, so you can eat one at a time and stop if your stomach complains. They also have a little salt, which can make you want to drink more water. They're low in protein and nutrients, so treat them as a bridge to a real meal.

**Should I eat toast or crackers first if I've been vomiting?**

Neither, at first. Start with small sips of water or an electrolyte drink every few minutes. Once fluids have stayed down for 15 to 30 minutes, try one or two crackers, which are easier to eat in tiny amounts, then move up to toast. If you can't keep any fluids down for more than about 12 hours, or you see blood in your vomit, get medical help.

**Does toast soak up alcohol?**

No. Bread doesn't absorb alcohol like a sponge, and by the morning most of the alcohol has usually already been absorbed and processed. Eating a full meal before drinking does slow how fast alcohol is absorbed, but a slice of toast alone isn't much of a buffer, and nothing you eat at the end of the night will sober you up faster.

**What's the best thing to put on toast for a hangover?**

Once your stomach can handle it, add something with protein or potassium: eggs, a thin layer of peanut butter, sliced banana, or avocado. A little honey is fine for quick sugar, though there is no good evidence it shortens a hangover. Go easy on butter, spicy spreads, and greasy sides while you're still queasy.

**Is white bread or whole grain better for a hangover?**

White bread is usually easier when you're nauseous because it's lower in fiber and moves through the stomach faster. Once you feel better, whole grain bread is the more nourishing choice, with more fiber, B vitamins, and minerals, and steadier energy through the day. Sourdough is a fine middle ground if you like it.

**Is the BRAT diet good for a hangover?**

Bananas, rice, applesauce, and toast are reasonable starting foods for a hangover because they're bland and easy to digest, and bananas add potassium. But they're low in protein and many nutrients, so use them for the first few hours and then return to normal meals as soon as your stomach allows rather than sticking to them all day.

**Can toast and crackers help hangover nausea?**

Many people find a small amount of bland food takes the edge off nausea, especially compared with an empty stomach. Eat slowly, a few bites at a time, sit upright, and keep sipping fluids. Ginger has better research behind it for nausea in general. If nausea is severe or lasts more than a day, talk to a doctor.
